title: Dusting high points, walls and vents
audience: Cleaners who dust ceilings, painted walls and air vents in offices and shared spaces.
learningOutcomes: Choose the right tool to reach ceilings, walls and vents.
Dust a painted wall, working downward, using a flat mop head and its pad, changing the pad when it is loaded.
Dust vents in line with their slats, and report any vent that cannot be reached safely.

instruction.heading: Choosing a tool for height
instruction.body: An extension duster lets you reach high surfaces from the floor. For painted walls, a flat mop fitted with a microfiber pad covers more area per pass than a duster does. Where dust is heavy or high up, a backpack vacuum fitted with a brush head, held on a long wand, lifts the dust away rather than moving it along.

instruction.heading: Walls
instruction.body: Adjust the mop so its head reaches the upper edge of the wall while the handle sits at a comfortable angle. Start beside the ceiling and draw the mop down in one vertical stroke to the skirting, then shift sideways and draw it up again. When you meet an obstacle, step around it with the mop and carry on to the upper edge. Keep working across the wall until the whole surface is covered, and swap the pad once it is visibly loaded.

instruction.heading: Vents
instruction.body: Fit a microfiber duster to a telescopic pole, or use a static duster that extends. Adjust the length so it reaches each vent. Sweep along the line of the vent's slats, so dust is carried along rather than pushed back into the grille. A heavily soiled vent may need a backpack vacuum with a brush head instead.

instruction.heading: Height and footing
instruction.body: Never stand on furniture, chairs or desks to reach a high point. Check what rests on the upper face of each shelf before you dust, so that nothing is knocked down onto you or the floor. If a high point is beyond the reach of your tools, do not improvise a platform. Report it to the site contact so that a safe method of access can be arranged.

procedure: Choose the tool for the surface: extension duster, flat mop with pad, or backpack vacuum.
Set the extension length so the working head reaches the surface without stretching.
For walls, draw the mop downward in vertical strokes, shift sideways, and work back up.
For vents, sweep the duster along the line of the slats.
Change pads when they are loaded, and return the tools to storage.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner needs to dust a vent above a tall filing cabinet, and the vent is out of reach of the extension duster.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not stand on the cabinet. Try a longer extension setting, or a backpack vacuum with a brush head worked from a safe position. If neither reaches the vent safely, record its location and report it to the site contact for a safe method of access.

equipmentAndPpe: Backpack vacuum with a brush head
Dust mask where dust is heavy

commonErrors.error: Standing on furniture to reach a high point.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the extension tool, or report the point for safe access.

commonErrors.error: Dusting a vent against the direction of its slats.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the slat direction on every pass.

commonErrors.error: Pushing dust down a wall in streaks.
commonErrors.prevention: Work in continuous strokes from the top, and swap the pad when it is loaded.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Wear eye protection when dusting overhead, because dust and debris fall downward.
Where dust is heavy, add a dust mask, and check that it fits the face before starting.
Do not work from unstable furniture or from any surface not designed to be stood on.

qualityStandard: Walls are dusted with no visible streaks.
Vents show no dust or cobwebs.
No items have been knocked down or moved out of place.
documentationEvidence: Tool changes and any access problems recorded on the route sheet.
summary: An extension duster suits high points, a flat mop with its pad suits walls, and a backpack vacuum suits heavy vent dust.
Work walls in continuous strokes from the top, and change pads when they are loaded.
Never stand on furniture; report any high point that needs safe access.

options: So dust is carried along rather than pushed back
Because the slats must be bent
Because vents cannot be dusted any other way
